entities.name: René Charles de Maupeou
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
René Charles de Maupeou, born in Paris on June 11, 1688, ascended through the ranks of the French judiciary to become Chancellor of France in 1768, serving until 1774. His pivotal, albeit ultimately unsuccessful, attempt to dismantle and reform the powerful sovereign courts, known as the *parlements*, during the final years of King Louis XV's reign, represents a critical episode in the struggle between royal absolutism and entrenched aristocratic privilege that defined the late Ancien Régime. Maupeou's actions were a desperate, top-down effort to restore fiscal solvency and strengthen monarchical authority, directly challenging institutions that had become formidable obstacles to royal reform and a de facto counter-power.

At the heart of Maupeou's tenure was the radical judicial reform initiated in 1771, often termed the 'Maupeou coup.' Confronted by the intransigence of the Parlement of Paris, which repeatedly obstructed royal edicts, particularly those related to taxation, Maupeou moved decisively. He exiled the recalcitrant magistrates, confiscated their offices, and replaced the traditional *parlements* with a new system of six superior councils (*conseils supérieurs*) whose judges were appointed and paid by the crown, thereby eliminating the venality of office and the right of remonstrance that had empowered the old courts. This sweeping reorganization aimed to streamline justice, reduce costs, and ensure the king's legislative will could be implemented without judicial obstruction, effectively centralizing power under the monarchy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: René Charles de Maupeou's radical judicial reforms represented a final, desperate attempt to salvage royal absolutism in France by dismantling the power of the *parlements*. His failure, due to the subsequent reversal by Louis XVI, critically weakened the monarchy's authority and ability to enact reform, directly contributing to the instability that led to the French Revolution.
